Your Best Work

No. 705 – November 1, 2026

Welcome to Brain Food, a weekly newsletter full of timeless ideas and insights you can use in life and work. (Read the archives). Not subscribed? Learn more and sign up.

Tiny Thoughts

Action produces the very information inaction waits for.

Being smart helps once you start. Before that, it often just makes your excuses more convincing.

Spite makes you work harder. Curiosity makes you work longer. Discipline is what you need when you have neither.



Insights

Michael Jordan on eliminating fear:*

“I never feared my skills because I put in the work. Work ethic eliminates fear.”

Gerry Spence on an underappreciated aspect of how we win:

“Winning is getting what we want, which often includes assisting others in getting what they want.”

Paul Graham on hitting the center of problems:

“Many problems have a hard core at the center, surrounded by easier stuff at the edges. Working hard means aiming toward the center to the extent you can. Some days you may not be able to; some days you’ll only be able to work on the easier, peripheral stuff. But you should always be aiming as close to the center as you can without stalling.”



The Knowledge Project

Steven Kotler and I sat down to talk about the science of doing your best work.

Kotler is a bestselling author and the executive director of the Flow Research Collective, where he studies the science of peak performance.

This episode is for anyone who wants to focus better, learn faster, or perform better. Check out the episode trailer.

issues.title: The Price of Admission
issues.html:
The Price of Admission

No. 704 – October 25th, 2026

Welcome to Brain Food, a weekly newsletter full of timeless ideas and insights you can use in life and work. (Read the archives). Not subscribed? Learn more and sign up.

Tiny Thoughts

The longer your email, the less likely it is to be read by someone who can act on it.

The price of admission to anything extraordinary isn’t talent or capital. It’s a willingness to be publicly bad at something for a while.

If you don’t know what will work, eliminate what won’t.

Often what looks like correct judgment in hindsight was avoiding obvious stupidity in the moment.



Insights

Olympian Eileen Gu on training:

“I train like I’ve never won, and I compete like I’ve never lost.”

In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna:

“You have the right to work, but never to the fruit of work. You should never engage in action for the sake of reward…Those who are motivated only by desire for the fruits of action are miserable, for they are constantly anxious about the results of what they do.”

Michael Bloomberg on small steps:

“Predicting the future’s impossible. You work hard because it increases the odds. But there’s no guarantee; much is dependent on what cards happen to get dealt. I have always believed in playing as many hands as possible, as intelligently as I can, and taking the best of what comes my way. Every significant advance I or my company has ever made has been evolutionary rather than revolutionary: small earned steps—not big lucky hits.”



The Knowledge Project

The Knowledge Project is one of the top business podcasts in the world.

The central idea is to “Master the best of what other people have already figured out.”

If you haven’t listened recently, you’re missing out.

issues.title: Defeat is Psychological
issues.html:
Defeat is Psychological

No. 703 – October 18th, 2026

Welcome to Brain Food, a weekly newsletter full of timeless ideas and insights you can use in life and work. (Read the archives). Not subscribed? Learn more and sign up.

Tiny Thoughts

The voice in your head is your ego’s defender. It shapes the facts to make you feel right.

“I don’t use Artificial Intelligence.”

A carpenter who refuses a hammer doesn’t make the house any better. He has only made his work slower and harder.

Judge the work, not the tool.

We spend time chasing money, then spend money chasing time.

Most of what you want when you finally have money is cheap: a slow morning, a walk with no destination, a day without meetings.

Real wealth is time.



Insights

Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius:

“Until death, all defeat is psychological.”

Ryan Serhant on becoming the person you want to be:

“Don’t act like the person you used to be. Act like the person you’re going to become.”

Edwin Land on the power of focus:

“My whole life has been spent trying to teach people that intense concentration for hour after hour can bring out in people resources they didn’t know they had.”



The Knowledge Project

Being good at what you do doesn’t guarantee that people will notice your work, trust you, or choose you.

That’s what I wanted to explore with this week’s guest, Ryan Serhant, founder of SERHANT. and star of Netflix’s Owning Manhattan.

We talk about getting noticed, earning trust, and asking for what you want without pushing people away. These skills matter whether you’re building a business, pitching an idea, or asking someone to take a chance on you.

Ryan also tells the story of a prospective client who didn’t reply for five years—and why he kept following up.

I’ve gotten more texts from close friends about this episode than any recent one. They all say some version of: “I didn’t think I would like this episode, but I learned so much. I’m listening again.”
